stops.name: Paris, the Course of Applied Aesthetics opens
stops.campa: In May 1839 Delsarte opens his Cours d'esthétique appliquée, the Course of Applied Aesthetics: the first systematic training of the expressive body in the Western theatre. To preachers, painters, singers, composers, orators and actors he teaches not tricks but LAW: the science of applied aesthetics, the grammar by which every inner state finds its true outward form. What the Conservatoire could not tell him, the WHY of gesture and tone, he now tells the age. The failed tenor has become the law-giver, and Paris comes to be taught its own body.
stops.quote: Eloquence is a means, not an end. We must not love art for its own sake, that would be idolatry. Art gives wings for ascent to God.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, in Delsarte System of Oratory

stops.name: The studio, the Law of Correspondence and the Trinity
stops.campa: In the studio the doctrine takes its shape. Man is threefold, life, mind, soul, after the image of the Trinity; and so his every faculty divides in three: the vocal, the buccal, and the gesture, the languages of what he feels, thinks and loves. The primary law is Correspondence: to each spiritual function answers a bodily form, eccentric, concentric or normal, so that from three genera spring nine species: the Universal Criterion that governs voice, speech and gesture alike. He teaches that gesture, being parallel with the impression, must always come first; speech is only reflected expression, after the fact.
stops.quote: Man says what he feels by inflections of the voice, what he loves by gesture, what he thinks by articulate speech.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, address before the Philotechnic Society, tr. Stebbins

stops.name: The studio, the nine attitudes and the zones
stops.campa: The grammar is drawn as a map on the living frame. The body divides into three zones: the head, mental; the torso, moral and emotive; the limbs, vital and physical. Every region bears its own ninefold accord, three directions crossed with three, so that the head alone owns nine attitudes, each the exact sign of a state of soul. Statics, dynamics, semiotics: the body at rest, the body in motion, the body as sign. What porcelain and hospital and Tuileries taught the eye is now set down as the Delsarte cross, the geometry of the expressive man.
stops.quote: Gesture must always precede speech. In fact, speech is reflected expression. It must come after gesture, which is parallel with the impression received.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, in Delsarte System of Oratory

stops.name: The salons, the great pupils gather
stops.campa: The famous course draws the age to Delsarte's rooms. The tragedienne Rachel comes; the English tragedian Macready; the singer Jenny Lind; the preacher Père Hyacinthe; the composers Gounod and Bizet cross his circle. He coaches orator and actor and priest to wed the inner feeling to the true gesture, to stop the forced style the Conservatoire had bred in him. In the salons he demonstrates rather than writes, singing the old airs with his ruined voice and moving so truly that hearers weep: the doctrine transmitted mouth to ear, body to eye, never fixed in a book.

stops.name: The court, recitals before the kings
stops.campa: The failed tenor sings before thrones. Delsarte performs at the courts of Louis-Philippe and of Napoleon III, drawing from a wrecked voice, by pure truth of expression, what golden throats cannot; France gives him the Legion of Honour. He proves in his own maimed person the whole thesis of his science: that the manner, the attitude, the felt and lawful gesture, moves the heart where mere sound fails. The wound of the Conservatoire is vindicated at the Tuileries palace: the ruined singer, become the master of expression, is honoured for the very lack that made him.

stops.name: The Sorbonne, the address before the Philotechnic Society
stops.campa: At the Sorbonne, before the Philotechnic Society of Paris, Delsarte delivers the one lecture the tradition keeps whole: the manuscript his widow will one day yield to his American heirs. There, in his own words, he sets the definitions the disciples will carry: gesture the direct agent of the heart, elliptical discourse; the three languages of feeling, thought and love; art not for itself but as wings for the ascent to God. The man who would not publish speaks his doctrine aloud once, plainly, and the spoken words become the scripture of the movement he founds.
stops.quote: Gesture is more than speech. It is the fit manifestation of feeling. It is the revealer of thought and the commentator upon speech.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, address before the Philotechnic Society of Paris

stops.name: Paris, Steele MacKaye at the master's feet
stops.campa: In October 1869 the young American Steele MacKaye comes to Paris and gives himself to Delsarte, studying with the master every day through to July 1870. The old man, ill and out of fashion, pours the unpublished science into this one devoted heir: the zones, the accords, the criterion, the whole grammar he never set in a book. To MacKaye he entrusts his papers and his trust. The disciple who will carry the doctrine across the ocean is being made in the very rooms where the war is about to fall.

stops.name: New York and Boston, the system reaches America
stops.campa: The war has driven MacKaye home. In March 1871, while the master lies dying in besieged Paris, the disciple mounts the platform in New York and Boston and introduces to America the Delsarte System: the first stone of every school of dance and drama that will rise from it. What Delsarte would not publish crosses the sea as living practice, adding harmonic gymnastics of MacKaye's own devising. The doctrine that began in a Tuileries garden, watching a child's thumb, now takes root in the New World even as its author's life runs out in the Old.

stops.name: Paris, the siege closes round the master
stops.campa: On the nineteenth of September 1870 the Prussian armies close the ring around Paris. Through the long hungry winter of the siege and into the burning spring of the Commune, the old master, ill and broken and out of fashion, holds on in the starving city. The empire whose court once honoured him has fallen; the pupils are scattered; the disciple is fled overseas. The scientist of the dying body now watches his own city die around him: the shells, the famine, the fire. He reads, in the great collective grief of Paris, the last confirmation of his lifelong law.

stops.name: Paris, the death of François Delsarte
stops.campa: On the twentieth of July 1871, in the wrecked and smoking aftermath of the Commune, François Delsarte dies in Paris: ill, broken, out of fashion, the great system still unpublished in his own hand. The failed tenor who lost his voice and gained a science, who read the law of the body off the dying and the grieving and a child's spread thumb, goes to his own death having given the whole movement-lineage its root. He is buried in the cemetery of Montmartre. The doctrine survives only because his widow keeps the papers and his heirs, across the sea, keep the practice.
stops.quote: Art gives wings for ascent to God.
stops.quote_source: François Delsarte, in Delsarte System of Oratory

stops.name: The world after: Stebbins, Laban, Muybridge and the notated body
stops.campa: The root sends up the tree. Genevieve Stebbins, MacKaye's pupil, obtains the Sorbonne manuscript from the widow and in 1885 publishes the Delsarte System of Expression, spreading harmonic gymnastics through America; from that soil rise Isadora Duncan, Ruth St. Denis, and the whole of modern dance. Laban will notate the moving body; Muybridge will freeze its every gesture in the frame; the grammar of expression Delsarte derived becomes the common inheritance of dance, film and theatre. The man who never published is the acknowledged father of the notated, expressive body.
